descriptors.R: nominee of the party of the administration in office since 1889
descriptors.D: nominee of the party that has held a majority in the House since the 1890 elections; himself President from 1885 to 1889
descriptors.O: nominee of a new third party founded by farmers' alliances and labor organizations, calling for free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax and government ownership of the railroads

others_line: Other candidates on some ballots, including a Prohibition and a Socialist Labor nominee (answer "other").
never_name: Harrison, Cleveland, Weaver, Reid, Stevenson, Field, Bidwell, McKinley or Blaine

slice_sources.men: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1892 (1890 from the published state tables; most 1890 schedules were later lost); men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1892 returns.
slice_sources.women: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1892 (1890 from the published state tables; most 1890 schedules were later lost); women 21+ outside the South; only Wyoming (a state since 1890) let women vote for president in 1892, so only Wyoming women cast a presidential vote.
slice_sources.south-white: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1892 (1890 from the published state tables; most 1890 schedules were later lost); white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1892 returns.
slice_sources.black-south: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1892 (1890 from the published state tables; most 1890 schedules were later lost); Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; legal disfranchisement had begun (Mississippi's 1890 constitution, poll taxes in Florida, Tennessee and Arkansas) on top of violence and fraud; the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.
slice_sources.immigrants: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1892 (1890 from the published state tables; most 1890 schedules were later lost); foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.
